opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think labeling matters even more in robotics than in language or vision, and the reason is that robotics data is so much more expensive and so much less abundant. With language models, you can scrape the internet and you get trillions of tokens. The internet is, in a sense, already labeled: people wrote text with intent, with structure. In robotics there's no internet of robot actions. Every trajectory has to be collected by someone teleoperating a robot, or recorded from a human demonstration, and that takes real time in the physical world.

So when each data point costs that much, how well you understand and annotate it becomes critical. A raw robot log is just camera frames, joint angles, and gripper states over time. On its own, that doesn't tell the model much. What was the robot trying to do? Where does one subtask end and the next begin? Was this attempt a success or a failure, and if it failed, why? Did the grasp slip, or was the object misidentified? Those annotations turn a pile of sensor streams into something a model can actually learn structure from.

There's also the language side. Today's robot foundation models are increasingly vision-language-action models, so you want to connect what the robot does to how a human would describe it: "pick up the red cup," "open the drawer halfway." Good language annotation at different levels of granularity, from high-level tasks down to low-level motions, is what lets these models generalize to new instructions instead of just memorizing trajectories.

And I'd add one thing people underestimate: quality and consistency. In robotics a small amount of noisy or inconsistent data can hurt a lot, because you don't have the sheer volume to average it out. If one operator labels the start of a grasp differently from another, or failed demos get mixed in as successes, the model picks up those inconsistencies. So a big part of the work isn't just labeling more, it's building the pipelines, the standards, and increasingly the automated tools, using vision-language models to pre-label and humans to verify, so the data is reliable at scale.

So for me, labeling is how you squeeze the most learning out of the scarcest resource in the field. If data is the bottleneck in robotics, annotation is how you widen it.

r001.rationale: The response says raw robot logs do not tell the model much on their own and that annotations make the sensor streams something the model can learn structure from.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that in robotics, the data is the product, in a way that's even more true than in language or vision. When you train a language model, the internet already exists. Somebody wrote all that text for their own reasons, and you just go collect it. Robotics doesn't have an internet. Nobody is out there naturally generating millions of trajectories of a robot arm folding laundry or opening a drawer. So every single piece of data you have, somebody had to deliberately go and create, and then somebody had to decide what it means.

That second part is where labeling and annotation come in, and I'd say it matters for a few reasons.

The first is that raw robot data is actually kind of meaningless on its own. You have a stream of joint angles, camera frames, force readings. If I just hand you a hundred hours of that, you can't do much. You need to know: what was the task here, where does one episode start and end, was this attempt successful or did the cup fall over, and if it failed, why did it fail. Annotation is what turns a pile of sensor logs into something a model can actually learn from.

The second reason is about language grounding. The models everyone is excited about now are the ones where you can tell the robot "put the red mug on the top shelf" and it does it. For that to work, you need the visual and motor data tied to language descriptions, and not just at the level of the whole task but ideally at the level of sub-steps. "Reach for the mug, grasp the handle, lift, move toward the shelf." That kind of fine-grained annotation is expensive, it's tedious, and it's exactly what makes the difference between a model that generalizes and one that only memorizes.

And the third thing, which I think people underrate, is quality control. When a human teleoperator collects demonstrations, some of those demonstrations are bad. They hesitate, they take a weird path, they bump into something. If you train on all of it indiscriminately, the robot learns the hesitations too. Labeling lets you filter, weight, and curate. In my experience, a smaller, cleaner, well-annotated dataset will beat a much bigger messy one almost every time.

So I'd put it this way: in robotics, the bottleneck isn't really the model architecture anymore. It's whether you have data that is good enough, and labeled well enough, for the architecture to learn anything useful from it.

r001.rationale: The response says raw robot sensor logs are hard to use on their own and that annotation turns them into data a model can learn from.

astra-6.text:
I think labeling and annotation are important because they connect what a robot senses to what we want it to understand and do. A camera gives you pixels, but those pixels don’t automatically tell you, “This is a cup, this is its handle, and this is a good place to grasp it.” Annotations give the learning system examples of those distinctions.

And in robotics, that understanding has physical consequences. Recognizing a cup is one thing; picking it up without dropping it or hitting something is another. So useful labels can go beyond object names to include position, motion, contact, or whether an action succeeded.

They also help us evaluate failures. Did the robot misunderstand the scene, or did it understand the scene and choose the wrong action? Good annotations help separate those problems. Not all robot learning requires manual labels, but reliable annotation gives us a foundation for both training and measuring progress.

r001.rationale: The response explains that raw camera pixels do not convey distinctions such as object identity or grasp points on their own, and that annotations give the learning system examples of those distinctions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think labeling and annotation are important because they connect the data a robot collects to what that data actually means. A camera gives you pixels, but the robot needs to understand: this is an object, this is a person, this is a surface I can grasp, and this is an obstacle I should avoid.

In robotics, that understanding has to lead to action in the physical world. So the quality and consistency of the annotations matter a lot. If the labels are ambiguous or incorrect, the robot can learn the wrong behavior. Good annotations also help us evaluate the system and understand where it fails, so we can improve it.

r001.rationale: The response explains that annotations give meaning to raw robot data and that annotation quality affects what behavior the robot learns.
